canonical_topic: REC price sensitivity to supply and demand
definition: Because RECs carry no intrinsic value, their price is driven entirely by the balance between regulator-mandated purchase requirements and available supply. When eligible supply is short relative to the requirement, prices rise toward the alternative compliance payment (the regulatory penalty for non-compliance) and stay elevated as long as the shortage persists; when supply exceeds the requirement, prices collapse toward zero as excess holders compete just to sell.
core_idea: REC prices behave as a bounded market between zero and the compliance penalty price, governed by quota supply/demand rather than production cost or physical commodity fundamentals.
key_points: The alternative compliance payment acts as an effective price ceiling
Sustained shortage keeps prices near the penalty price
Oversupply drives prices toward zero (example: 10 million RECs created but only 2 million required leads sellers to bid near zero)

RECs and similar environmental products generally: have no inherent value, derive demand purely from regulatory compliance needs, are highly sensitive to supply/demand shifts, and are only usable within the specific jurisdiction of the regulator that created the requirement
relationships: Interacts directly with RPS-set purchase requirements and the alternative compliance payment penalty level
trading_implications: REC price risk is primarily regulatory/quota risk, not fuel-cost or weather-driven risk
Traders need to track eligible generation supply against the mandated requirement rather than production economics
caveats: REC prices are not anchored to generation cost — a REC can trade near zero even if the underlying generation was costly, if supply overshoots the mandate
